stories.body:
Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Business live – latest updates

Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy .

The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. Wachtell’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management.

Nvidia did not give a timeframe for the investigation but the company has said Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”.

The company is reeling from an espionage scandal after reports that its chief executive had been having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was also an Nvidia customer.

The US ambassador to China , David Perdue, said: “The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent.

“National security is part of this economic conversation because economic security is national security. And so, what we’re doing with China is bumpy right now,” he told Bloomberg Television.

Nvidia had at first denied an improper relationship with the Chinese citizen, who is no relation to the Nvidia boss, but Huang then admitted on Sunday he had been unfaithful to his wife – without referring directly to Ms Huang.

On the same day Nvidia announced an investigation into reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. The scandal has wiped $430bn off Nvidia’s value as shareholders gauge the potential impact of the scandal on a company and an executive who are synonymous with the AI boom.

Wachtell is one of the most prestigious corporate law firms in the US. Its founding partner Martin Lipton invented the “poison pill defence” in the 1980s, a corporate gambit that helps companies ward off hostile takeovers.

Technically called the “shareholder rights plan”, the poison pill allowed investors to buy more shares at a discount if one shareholder acquired a certain percentage of the company’s stock. This made it harder for corporate raiders to acquire a company without the board’s approval.

The firm was closely involved in the takeover of Getty Oil by Texaco. This was the largest corporate takeover in history at the time, although it turned sour when the thwarted suitor Pennzoil sued Texaco and won.

In 2008, a team of Wachtell lawyers advised the US Treasury department on the takeover of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac during the financial crisis.

The company was founded in the 1960s and is said to be the most profitable law firm in the US. It pulled in revenues of $5.1m per lawyer last year and made profits of $12m per partner, the highest profits per partner ever, according to the Am Law 100 rankings .

From 2017 to 2018, Kim was the acting US attorney for the southern district of New York, where he ran a team of lawyers investigating securities and commodities fraud, mail and wire fraud, public and private corruption, money laundering, cybercrime, and tax offences.

after newsletter promotion

That included the case of the former US representative Anthony Weiner , who was sentenced to 21 months in prison for sending obscene material to a minor.

He also oversaw the prosecution of the banker Mehmet Hakan Atilla, who was convicted in 2017 of helping to evade US sanctions on Iran .

Another high-profile assignment landed on Kim’s desk in 2021, when he investigated multiple allegations of sexual harassment by the then New York governor, Andrew Cuomo.

One analyst has put Huang’s chances of leaving Nvidia at 15%.

“Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the board investigation is completed,” wrote the tech analyst Dan Ives in a note to investors. “We would expect a board investigation that could take four weeks to six weeks and will create a clear overhang on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia.”

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and the founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, has put Huang’s survival chances at “about 50-50”.

stories.title: Trump wanted little Kei trucks for America, Toyota makes it happen
stories.summary: Does this herald the start of a small car revolution, or is it a meaningless distraction?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Does this herald the start of a small car revolution, or is it a meaningless distraction?

The idea that Americans should be offered a greater choice of smaller cars has support from strange bedfellows indeed. After all, who could forget President Trump—usually one to take a maximalist approach to any problem— announcing last year that he wanted the Department of Transportation to make Japan’s diminutive “Kei” cars legal here in the US.

Ars’ attempts to get DoT to tell us more about the potential influx of little vehicles have mostly fallen on deaf ears. But this week, there has been movement on the topic, with Toyota announcing that it will bring back the Scion brand with the KEI-01.

What’s a Kei car?

Here in the US, the preponderance of humongous SUVs is a consequence largely of government policies, specifically corporate average fuel economy standards that made it less profitable to sell smaller, efficient cars. Japan’s Kei cars are what happens if the government instead restricts the size, engine capacity, and power output.

A Kei car must fit within the following dimensions: 11.2 feet (3.4 m) long, 4.9 feet (1.5 m) wide, and 6.6 feet (2 m) tall, with an engine displacement of no more than 0.66 L and an output of 63 hp (47 kW) or less. That’s a far cry from the more than 16 feet (4.9 m) of a full-size pickup truck, but it makes sense for a country where you’re not allowed to buy a car unless you have somewhere to park it, with those spaces being at an absolute premium.

Being affordable to buy and economical to run sure doesn’t hurt either, and last year, Japan bought almost 1.7 million Kei cars, out of total sales of 4.6 million vehicles. Depending on where you live in the US, it can be varying degrees of difficult to import a Kei car , at least until now.

Scion is back?

Toyota killed off its Scion sub-brand more than a decade ago , ending the haggle-free approach and cars aimed at younger buyers in favor of selling more Toyotas. But now it’s back as “Scion by Toyota,” which the automaker will apparently use to experiment with less traditional ideas. But forget about a cool-but-boxy EV in the mold of the Honda N-One or Nissan Sakura .

“The future of mobility will not be defined by one vehicle, one technology, or one way of thinking,” said Simon Humphries, Toyota’s chief branding officer and head of design. “Scion by Toyota gives us a place to challenge conventional thinking, explore new possibilities, and create mobility in new ways. The KEI-01, SxS, and BKE concepts each represent a different possibility—and together, they show what can happen when curiosity leads the way.”

Before anyone gets too excited, the KEI-01 will be classified as a “ low-speed vehicle ,” which means it can’t go any faster than 25 mph (40 km/h). So if you were hoping to use one of these but need to drive on anything but surface streets, be prepared to get honked at, a lot, and not in a good way. In fact, unless you’re buying a fleet, Toyota won’t sell you a KEI-01 at all, at least not to begin with.

Oh, and it’s only available as right-hand drive, since that’s the side of the road Japan drives on. But it does feature all-wheel drive, so if you own a ranch—or perhaps a whole load of golf courses—the utility becomes a little more obvious. Toyota says the KEI-01 is suited to small business owners in urban environments, farmers and ranchers, organizations that have campuses that need fleets of facility vehicles, delivery drivers, and outdoor enthusiasts. The trucks will be shipped to Toyota’s assembly plant in Indiana as knock-down kits, adding 50 jobs to the plant in mid-2027.

Low-speed vehicles have been street-legal in parts of the US for many years now. In my neighborhood in Washington, DC, Circuit operates a low-speed EV shuttle on demand, and gas-powered golf carts are very popular in retirement communities. Pricing for the KEI-01 hasn’t been announced, but speculation runs from as little as $10,000 to as much as $28,000.

stories.title: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
stories.summary: Some people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland can get help with heating costs during cold spells.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 9 February 2021

As temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments.

This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures.

In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets.

What are cold weather payments?

The cold weather payment is a government benefit top-up to help with fuel bills , external .

The average temperature in a local area must be recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven days in a row.

The temperature is recorded by the relevant weather station for your postcode.

England and Wales: Enter your postcode here to check eligibility , external

Northern Ireland: Enter your postcode here to check eligibility , external

More than 1.4 million cold weather payments were made during winter 2025-26.

Check the UK weather warnings in place

Who can get cold weather payments and how much are they worth?

To qualify, you must live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland.

Payments are not age-related but you must already be receiving certain benefits, including:

pension credit

income support

income-based job seekers' allowance

income-related employment and support allowance

universal credit - although there are certain exceptions

support for mortgage interest

Each cold weather payment is for a seven-day period and is worth £25.

More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather.

The scheme runs between 1 November and 31 March each year.

Hospital stays can affect your entitlement to the payment so you should tell the Pension Service , external or Jobcentre Plus , external if you become an inpatient.

You should also update the relevant service if you have a baby, or if a child under five comes to live with you.

In Scotland, the winter heating payment is worth £62 , external , and is paid automatically between December and February.

Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed Published 2 January

How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips Published 2 January

How to drive in snow and icy weather Published 2 January

How do cold weather health alerts work? Published 22 June

How do I get cold weather payments and how long does it take?

You do not have to do anything in order to receive cold weather payments.

The money should be paid automatically into the same bank or building society account as your benefits, within two weeks of the qualifying period of cold weather.

If you do not receive a payment, you can contact the Pension Service , external or Jobcentre Plus , external .

Cold weather payments do not affect other benefits.

They are separate to the winter fuel payment , which is worth £100 or £300 depending on your individual circumstances.

About nine million pensioners get the Winter Fuel Payment, after a government u-turn over changes to the eligibility rules.

‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’

Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.

One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of Democrats ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back Donald Trump ’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.

Early odds suggest a Democrat may win the presidential election in two years, a fitting coda to last week’s broad rejection of the Maga brand of politics. It’s not beyond hope to expect a Democratic trifecta that will spend less time on settling grievances and more on fixing a threadbare social safety net that allows for the deepest poverty in the affluent world .

And yet, the post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money. The federal deficit is now running at about 6.2% of GDP . The federal debt hit $40tn, more than 120% of the nation’s gross domestic product. Paying interest on that debt costs some 3.2% of GDP. That’s about $1tn, more than is spent on national defense. The Congressional Budget Office projects that debt and interest payments will continue to grow faster than the economy over the coming decades. In October alone, the first month of the 2027 fiscal year, the fiscal deficit ballooned to $409bn.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that restoring the subsidies to health insurance plans under Obamacare from 2030 to 2039 would cost $460bn. Undoing the budget cuts to the Snap food stamp program and Medicaid that Trump used to partly fund the tax cuts in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would cost $2.2tn over that decade. “Reversing the harms is going to be very expensive,” said CBPP’s senior director for Federal budget policy, Brendan Duke.

And that’s the easy part. The trust fund that pays for social security benefits is scheduled to run out of money in less than six years, when the new crop of Democratic senators are still in their first term. By law, that would lead to an automatic 22% cut in benefits. Fixing that will require more money. Artificial intelligence may further complicate the picture, burdening the safety net with potentially millions of workers displaced by the new technological revolution.

Historian Bruce Bartlett, who back in the day advised Ronald Reagan on budget policy, argues that this state of affairs is the outcome of a Republican strategy honed over the years since Gipper’s day: cut taxes to strangle the budget and tie the hands of whatever Democratic administration comes next.

Trump’s OBBBA will add somewhere between $4.1tn and $5.5tn to the federal debt over 10 years, depending on whether temporary tax cuts in the bill are made permanent by a future Congress, something that has usually happened in the past. This, Bartlett once told me , will “make sure the next Democratic president is a complete and total failure”.

The new taxes that would be needed just to fill the holes Trump and his Republican enablers bored into the budget, let alone patch up the safety net they gleefully eviscerated, seem beyond anything achieved in recent memory.

Consider this: The last time that a government with any Republican in power delivered a tax increase was in the 1990s, when George HW Bush was president and Congress was blue. Bush paid for his sin, though, losing reelection to Democrat Bill Clinton. And that was the end of that.

Democrats have raised money when they held the presidency and Congress. But the trend suggests the opportunities are fading. Bill Clinton’s 1993 tax increases are estimated to yield the equivalent of $3.3tn over the 2030-2039 decade, adjusting for inflation. But the feat, which helped produce the nation’s first budget surplus since the 1960s, was ultimately spent on a tax cut by Clinton’s successor, George W. Bush.

The next shot at raising taxes was more modest. Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act raised the equivalent of $1.1tn over 2030-2039, in inflation-adjusted dollars. But Obama also made permanent some of George W Bush’s tax cuts. Joe Biden tried to go bigger: his original Build Back Better Act, passed in the House, would have raised the equivalent of $2.3tn over that window. But the Senate nixed that, authorizing only about $700bn in the Inflation Reduction Act.

How much more tax revenue does the US need? It depends on what Democrats want to achieve. Total tax revenue in the US amounts to less than 26% of its gross domestic product. That is 9 percentage points less than Britain’s total tax take, as a share of its economy, 9.5 points less than Canada’s, 12.5 points less than Germany’s and 16 percentage points less than Sweden’s.

Perhaps matching other rich countries is an impossibly high bar. Still, Democrats must prove that they understand the new America they hope to build comes with a price tag they are willing to fight for.

Some tax cuts in Trump’s OBBBA are set to expire in the next couple of years: exemptions on income from tips and overtime, a new deduction for seniors and an increase in the deduction for state and local taxes. The CBPP observed that these cuts offer next to nothing to Americans on the bottom rungs of the income distribution. Extending them would cost about $1.2tn over the 10-year window.

Will Democrats have the guts to end them? That will be the test of whether America is ready for a new social contract or not.

stories.title: Burnham signals backing for more ethnicity options on next census
stories.summary: It comes after a Lib Dem MP said black English or Asian English should be specific options for respondents.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 minutes ago

Andy Burnham has signalled his support for dedicated options at the next census to allow people to define themselves as black English or Asian English.

It comes after Liberal Democrat MP Josh Babarinde called for legislation to widen ethnicity options for respondents at the next population count, due in 2031.

The last census, held in 2021, saw English offered within a broader white category, but without specific options for black English or Asian English.

Asked at Prime Minister's Questions whether he would support Babarinde's proposal, Burnham said he had not seen details of the plan.

But he added: "I stand here thinking that I would want to support that bill, to directly take on the poisonous politics we've seen from some in this House".

"We must bring people back together. I am interested in working with anyone in this House who shares that aim," he added.

Burnham did not respond to a follow-up question from Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey about whether he would meet Babarinde to discuss his plan, and he did not specify whether the government would give it time for debate in Parliament.

Babarinde introduced his proposal for legislation on Tuesday, under a rule that allows MPs to propose new laws in a 10-minute speech.

Such draft laws, known as private members' bills, rarely become law without support from the government of the day but are often used by MPs to raise awareness of issues and generate media attention for policy ideas.

Census should include black English and Asian English options, says MP Published 17 hours ago

Respondents to the 2021 census were asked a two-stage question about ethnicity, with options grouped under five broad ethnic headings.

In Wales, the terms "Asian Welsh" and "Black Welsh" were listed in the broad categories themselves, and respondents were able to pick "Welsh" as an option underneath the broader white category.

The form in England listed "English" as an option in the white ethnic category, but the only way for respondents to describe themselves as Black English or Black English was via a free-form text box.

In Scotland, the term "Scottish Asian" appeared in the broad categories, whilst "Black Scottish" was given as an example response for the text box.

Speaking on Tuesday, Babarinde said his proposed law would introduce Black English and Asian English as specific new categories, arguing that the text box on the current form "may as well be the margin".

Braverman 'Englishness' remarks

Babarinde's proposal has been backed by some MPs in other parties, including Labour former deputy prime minister David Lammy and Conservative Sir James Cleverly, who quit the shadow cabinet this summer to run for London mayor.

The Eastbourne MP has previously told the BBC he put forward his bill in the wake of comments by former Conservative home secretary Suella Braverman, who defected to Reform UK earlier this year.

Braverman wrote in 2015 , external that she was British Asian but said she "cannot claim to be English" despite being born and educated in England.

She has reaffirmed her position in recent weeks, writing on X that Englishness was "an ethnicity" and it was "not racist to say this".

"To say I'm English is to take a 'laissez-faire, anything-goes' attitude to ethnicity, citizenship and identity. It also denies me my Asian heritage," she added.

The detailed questions asked during the census in England and Wales are set out in legislation following recommendations from the Office of National Statistics.

The law setting out the questions for the last census was passed around 10 months before it took place in March 2021. The Scottish government delayed the census in Scotland until the following year because of the Covid pandemic.

stories.title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
stories.summary: Ukraine competes with Russia and data centers for China’s optical fiber supply.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ukraine competes with Russia and data centers for China’s optical fiber supply.

Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones.

Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider .

Ukraine and Russia have been producing an estimated 50,000 fiber-optic drones per month in recent years. That’s a lot of optical fiber that has effectively become a one-time battlefield consumable.

But China’s economic and security ties with Russia have enabled Russia to import significantly larger amounts of fiber-optic cable than Ukraine—at least according to China’s official customs data. For example, Russia imported 328,000 miles of fiber-optic cable from China in August 2025 alone, compared to Ukraine getting just 72 miles of cable from Chinese companies, according to The Washington Post .

To get a better sense of how drone warfare has increased demand for optical fiber technology, Russia alone bought more than 37 million miles (60 million kilometers) of fiber-optic cable in 2025, according to The Insider and Russian business publication Vedomosti . That means Russia’s purchases amounted to more than 10 percent of all fiber produced worldwide last year, when it had previously never accounted for more than 1 percent of global demand.

The global AI boom and ongoing data center buildout have also strained optical fiber supply, with an expected worldwide shortfall of 111 million miles (180 million kilometers) in 2026, according to the market research firm TrendForce . That has further increased the cost of optical fiber purchased by Russia and Ukraine, including the bend-insensitive fiber that is especially coveted for fiber-optic drones.

One Ukrainian drone manufacturer navigating these supply-chain challenges is BlueBird Tech, which produces fiber-optic drones along with other military drones, a ground robot, drone detection systems, and electronic warfare systems. Ars reached out to BlueBird Tech to learn more.

The following Q&A represents written responses from Oleksiy, a BlueBird Tech R&D representative, after an initial conversation with Ars. The responses have been lightly edited for clarity. Oleksiy is only being identified by first name for security reasons.

Ars Technica: How has the use of fiber-optic drones by Ukraine and Russia evolved, and where does the technology stand today?

Oleksiy: Fiber-optic drones are a specific type of drone used for particular operations. One of their main characteristics is that they do not produce the same radio-frequency (RF) emissions as conventional RF-controlled FPV drones. That means conventional RF detectors cannot detect them in the same way, and electronic warfare systems cannot disrupt their control link in the same way either.

At the same time, fiber-optic drones have their own operational limitations. A pilot who is experienced with a conventional RF-controlled FPV drone cannot necessarily switch immediately to a fiber-optic drone. It requires specific skills, and fiber-optic drones have different flight characteristics.

So there are significant advantages, particularly when operating in an electronic warfare environment, but there are also limitations in terms of operation, pilot training, and cost.

Because of the high density of electronic intelligence and electronic warfare systems on the battlefield, using conventional radio-controlled FPV drones has become increasingly difficult.

Fiber-optic technology provides a way to operate in these conditions, although it also comes with certain limitations.

So today, both sides are using fiber-optic drones on the battlefield, but radio-controlled drones still make up the larger share overall.

Ars Technica: What are the main disadvantages or limitations of fiber-optic drones?

Oleksiy: One of the biggest limitations today is cost. If we compare fiber-optic prices in 2025 and 2026, we have seen increases of roughly six to 10 times. The most difficult period in terms of prices and shortages was around March. Since then, the situation has stabilized to some extent.

But the underlying issue remains that the material primarily comes from China. That means Ukrainian manufacturers depend on Chinese supply, logistics, availability, and pricing.

There is also broader global demand for fiber-optic material. FPV drones are only one application. Data centers around the world consume large amounts of fiber, and the growth of AI infrastructure is also contributing to demand.

So Ukrainian drone manufacturers are operating within a much larger global market for fiber optic, and that affects both availability and price.

Ars Technica: How are Ukrainian manufacturers adapting to these supply-chain and quality challenges?

Oleksiy: One important change is that many manufacturers are moving the spooling process in-house. Instead of buying a finished fiber-optic spool for an FPV drone, they can buy the fiber in much larger spools and produce the smaller drone spools themselves.

This does not remove the dependence on China for the material itself, but it gives manufacturers more control over the finished product.

Quality is a major reason for doing this. We have seen problems and defects in finished spools supplied from China. By doing the spooling themselves, manufacturers can introduce their own quality-control procedures and achieve a more consistent result.

It can also make the finished spool somewhat cheaper than buying a finished product in China and transporting it to Ukraine.

But quality is the most important factor. If a fiber-optic spool has a defect, you can lose the drone, lose the mission, and lose the target.

Fiber optic is also not the only component in this supply chain. Media converters are another component manufacturers need to source, and China is important for that supply as well.

Ars Technica: So Ukrainian companies are buying large quantities of fiber and producing the FPV spools domestically?

Oleksiy: Yes. A manufacturer can buy a large spool of fiber-optic material and then use that material to produce smaller spools designed for FPV drones.

That also allows the manufacturer to perform its own quality checks during production rather than relying entirely on the quality of a finished imported spool.

Ars Technica: Has this become the standard approach across the Ukrainian industry?

Oleksiy: It depends on the manufacturer and on the size of the company. Larger companies may have the resources to do the spooling themselves. That requires spooling equipment, people who understand the process, testing capabilities, and quality control.

Smaller manufacturers may not have those resources. In those cases, they may buy finished spools from larger Ukrainian manufacturers or from suppliers abroad, including China.

So there is no single model across the industry. It largely depends on the scale and capabilities of each manufacturer.

Ars Technica: Can Ukraine source fiber-optic material from countries other than China?

Oleksiy: You can buy fiber-optic material through suppliers in other countries, but in practice China remains the main source in this market.

There can be intermediaries in other countries, and prices can differ depending on the country and the purchasing route.

But in the end, China remains the main source of the fiber-optic material we are talking about.

Ars Technica: Have Ukrainian companies experienced actual shortages or situations where suppliers were unable or unwilling to fill orders?

Oleksiy: Yes, there have been situations like that. It depends on many factors, including how the material is purchased, which supplier is involved, and the logistics.

There have also been cases where Chinese manufacturers have told Ukrainian buyers that they did not have material available for them because they were from Ukraine.

Russia also has more direct logistics with China, so from a practical supply-chain perspective it has an easier route for sourcing this material.

Ars Technica: Are there other important supply-chain challenges beyond availability and price?

Oleksiy: Yes. Logistics is another important factor. Once the material reaches Ukraine, it still has to pass through customs and then be transported to manufacturers.

Air raid alerts can interrupt this process. Customs operations and other parts of the logistics chain may stop during alerts, which adds time before the material reaches the manufacturer. So companies have to take these delays into account when planning production.

There are also security considerations. I cannot discuss specific cases involving attacks on fiber-optic production because of security restrictions. But manufacturers are potential targets for the enemy, so security measures are extremely important for developers, suppliers, and manufacturers.

Ars Technica: Is the physical transportation route from China to Ukraine also a challenge?

Oleksiy: Yes. The route from China to Ukraine is much longer, and that creates challenges in terms of both time and logistics costs.

So the problem is not only obtaining the material itself. Manufacturers also have to account for the time and expense required to transport it over a long distance.

Ars Technica: How do these price, logistics, and supply-chain challenges affect how a drone manufacturer approaches fiber-optic systems?

Oleksiy: Planning becomes extremely important. You need to plan production and logistics together. If you understand your manufacturing requirements in advance, you can plan your logistics and your next orders accordingly.

Having more of the manufacturing process under your own control is also important.

Quality is another major factor. If the fiber has fewer defects, you can produce more usable FPV spools from one large spool of material. If there are many defects, you ultimately produce fewer usable spools from the same amount of fiber.

So production planning, logistics planning, in-house manufacturing capabilities, material quality, and the skills of the people doing the work are all closely connected.

Ars Technica: Does producing fiber-optic spools require specially trained personnel?

Oleksiy: Yes. We do not have universities that specifically train people to manufacture these FPV fiber-optic spools. So it comes down to training, training, and more training.

When people first learn the process, they naturally make mistakes and create defects. They need practical experience to improve.

Training itself also consumes fiber-optic material because people have to practice the actual manufacturing process.

So developing skilled personnel is another part of scaling production. The goal is to develop the skills required to manufacture consistently high-quality spools with as few defects as possible.

Ars Technica: What makes manufacturing a fiber-optic spool technically difficult?

Oleksiy: You need to understand a lot about the fiber itself, about the spooling process, and about what happens when the fiber unwinds from the spool during operation.

Fiber-optic cable is fragile and can be damaged or broken relatively easily. If something goes wrong during manufacturing or while the fiber is unwinding, you can damage the fiber and lose the connection.

That is why practical experience is so important. You need to practice the manufacturing process, and that can require many kilometers of fiber just for training.

The equipment used for spooling also matters. If you use low-quality equipment or the equipment is not configured properly, you can introduce more defects into the finished spool.

So both the equipment and the people operating it affect the quality of the final product.

Ars Technica: How automated is the spooling process?

Oleksiy: It depends on the type of equipment. Some systems require more manual involvement, while others are more automated.

But even with automated equipment, skilled personnel are still required. Someone has to configure the equipment correctly and understand how the process works. The way the system is set up also affects the quality of the finished product.

So automation does not remove the need for expertise.

Ars Technica: How do manufacturers test the quality of finished fiber-optic spools?

Oleksiy: There are different levels of testing. Every finished spool should be checked to make sure the optical link itself is working properly.

But if you want to ensure consistent production quality, that is not enough. You also need to take a portion of the finished spools from a production batch, install them on actual FPV drones, and fly them under real conditions.

That allows you to test not only the optical connection itself, but also whether the finished spool performs properly during an actual flight.

So every spool should undergo link testing, while some of the finished spools from each production batch should also be tested in real flights. That combination is important if you want to maintain consistent quality in production.

Manufacturer says ‘shift to new energy vehicles is happening faster than expected’ and market is harsh

Business live – latest updates

The Japanese carmaker Nissan has said it has been caught out by accelerating sales of electric and hybrid cars in China amid a brutal price war in the world’s biggest automotive market.

The manufacturer slashed its sales forecasts for China and said it would cut back on petrol car manufacturing while increasing production of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, which combine a smaller battery with a petrol engine.

Nissan said it expected to sell between 2.97m and 3m cars this year, down from a previous forecast of 3.15m, mainly because of struggles in China.

“China remains our biggest challenge,” said Ivan Espinosa, Nissan’s chief executive. “Demand is weaker, competition is intensifying, and the shift to new energy vehicles is happening faster than expected. The market is being very, very harsh.”

The company reported increased sales in its home market as well as in North America, regions in which the shift to electric cars has been much slower because of policy decisions, including Donald Trump’s tearing up of incentives for battery car makers.

That divergence between different parts of the world illustrates the challenge for global carmakers, many of whom are trying to continue selling their more profitable petrol and diesel cars for as long as possible while risking being left behind by newer Chinese rivals .

China’s government gave weighty subsidies to its electric car industry, spotting an opportunity to overtake other countries such as Germany, Japan and the US, which had dominated sales of internal combustion engine cars.

That led to a huge number of Chinese EV competitors, which are now chasing a shrinking market. Nissan said sales across China fell by 22% in the first half of the year. That pressure “intensified from July through October” and left the carmaker’s sales down 32% in the first nine months of the year, Nissan said.

Espinosa said Nissan’s product lineup in China, led by the Sylphy family of saloon cars, was too heavily associated with petrol engines, so the company was cutting local production, exporting some products, while trying to ramp up its N series of models, which are electric or plug-in hybrids.

Yet at the same time as pushing for increased electric car production in China, Nissan has been among the manufacturers slowing the shift to batteries in Europe. In the UK the carmaker has lobbied to weaken the zero-emission vehicle mandate , a target for increasing EV sales, and to continue to sell petrol cars after 2035 .

after newsletter promotion

That lobbying came despite evidence of rising demand for electric cars in the UK, particularly since the Iran war pushed up petrol and diesel prices. Data this week showed that sales of used electric vehicles rose much faster than petrol cars.

Ian Plummer, the chief customer officer at the car sales website Autotrader, said: “The standout trend in the used car market is the rapid rise of retail sales of electric vehicles, up an eye-popping 56% year on year in October and now accounting for one in 10 retail sales on Autotrader.”

Nissan’s only European factory is in Sunderland in northern England. Espinosa said he was hopeful that the company’s products from Sunderland and Japan would be included in proposed “Made in Europe” rules from the EU . The rules as drafted would exclude all of Nissan’s cars from subsidies and other incentives within the EU, adding to pressure on the carmaker.

stories.title: Reform boycotts Senedd after member banned for saying white people are being replaced
stories.summary: Party members withdrew from most of Wednesday's Senedd proceedings over Joe Martin's speaking ban.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reform UK Wales member Joe Martin, party leader Helen Jenner and chief whip Llŷr Powell announced the boycott on the Senedd's steps

Published 11 November 2026, 11:47 GMT

Reform UK will partially boycott the Senedd to protest the ban of one of their politicians for claiming white people are being "replaced".

The party's Welsh leader, Helen Jenner, said Joe Martin's ban was because of "undue pressure" from governing party Plaid Cymru and was an "infringement on freedom of speech".

Martin had been told he would not be allowed to speak in the Senedd's chamber until he apologised for the remarks, which the parliament's Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called the ruling "ridiculous and outrageous".

Reform, which is by far the Senedd's largest opposition party, said its members would withdraw from most of Wednesday's proceedings before returning to vote in the parliament later in the evening.

Reform's Joe Martin given Senedd speaking ban after he said white people are being replaced Published 21 hours ago

Jenner confirmed her party's boycott on the steps of the Senedd on Wednesday afternoon.

"It is now clear that the freedom of speech of one of our Senedd members is being curtailed, meaning his constituents are being silenced," she said.

"We stand behind Joe, and we will not attend today's plenary session in protest at his treatment.

"Every Reform MS [Member of the Senedd] will be in their Senedd office working hard for our constituents."

Martin said he would not apologise.

"My voters sent me to the Senedd to speak on their behalf," he said.

"I am being blocked from doing so, and now it's clear that I have fewer rights than the people who elected me. That cannot be the situation in a national parliament."

Asked by BBC Wales if he genuinely believed white people were being "replaced" in the UK, Martin said: "That's obviously a fact."

Joe Martin was told he would not be called to speak until he apologised

Posting on X, Farage said it was "ridiculous and outrageous that Reform's duly elected Member of the Senedd, Joe Martin, has been banned from speaking in the Welsh Parliament".

"Why is it only Reform that's targeted like this?" he asked.

Martin was also backed by the leader of right-wing party Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe.

He called for the Senedd to be "shut down" if it was "going to shut down legitimate debate around demographic security and immigration".

Martin's Caerdydd Penarth constituency includes some of Wales' most ethnically diverse communities.

Farage announced Jenner as his party's Welsh leader at the Senedd in September

On Tuesday Martin asked for a Welsh government statement on the "demographic replacement of white British people" during business questions, when Senedd members are free to raise issues they choose.

Business Minister Heledd Fychan immediately asked the presiding officer whether the remarks were within the Senedd's standing orders - a set of rules that govern conduct in the chamber.

Standing orders give the presiding officer discretion to decide if contributions to plenary sessions - meetings of the full Senedd - use "discriminatory or offensive language".

Delivering his ruling later, Irranca-Davies said: "Until I receive a clear indication that the member understands the boundaries of acceptable parliamentary conduct and apologises to the Siambr [chamber], we will not be calling him to speak."

Senedd officials confirmed an apology would have to be made in the chamber during a plenary session.

The ruling does not cover committees.

Martin is a member of the Senedd's Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee.

Irranca-Davies pointed out it was not the first time he has rebuked Martin. In September, he said Martin had made offensive remarks about surgeons working in the Welsh NHS gender service .

Plaid Cymru Senedd member Carrie Harper called Reform's boycott a "pathetic tantrum" that was a "disgrace to democracy".

"They'd rather play gimmicks and chase headlines than be serious about Wales' future and doing the job they were elected to do on behalf of the people they represent," she said.

In the 2021 census 93.8% of people in Wales identified as white, down from 95.6% a decade earlier, with the country's overall population growing by 1.4% to 3,107,500.

The proportion identifying as Asian, Asian Welsh or Asian British, the next highest group in the survey, rose from 2.3% to 2.9%.

Mixed or multiple ethnic groups rose from 1% to 1.6%, and those identifying as Black, Black Welsh, Black British, Caribbean or African rose from 0.6% to 0.9%.

stories.title: We’re Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
stories.summary: Today , along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant , a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places. But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin , ALPRs give law enforcement “ a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “ form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment. We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant. Related Cases: Wisconsin Council of Churches v. Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha & Green Bay SIREN and CAIR-CA v. San Jose

stories.title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
stories.summary: The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies. The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying. Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system. In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only 37 IPR petitions were filed in September 2026, compared to 129 petitions in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges. This dramatic decline shouldn’t just concern patent lawyers. EFF has fought bad patents because so many software and internet patents make claims to the basic tools of free expression online, like sending email, using online ads, or publishing web pages. When bad patents go unchallenged, they affect everyone who cares about the freedom to write new code and make new technology. That’s why EFF has defended IPR since it came on the scene more than a decade ago. It provides a faster and less expensive way to challenge patents that should never have been granted. Congress created IPRs because the Patent Office makes mistakes. District court litigation is an extraordinarily expensive way to correct them. Without a meaningful administrative review process, bad patents remain powerful weapons in the hands of patent trolls and others seeking to extract settlements from companies that often did nothing wrong. Now, USPTO leadership is dismantling that safeguard. stories.title: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?
stories.summary: As Hollywood begins to adopt the technology, the professionals in most direct jeopardy are the illustrators mapping out directors’ first visions. They sketch out what could be lost A film industry dominated by AI is a dystopian prospect: stories and dialogue generated by large language models, populated by reincarnated screen icons and uncanny humanoids . That is in the future, but the real-world impact of AI is already directly affecting jobs behind the scenes, as Hollywood’s biggest film-makers begin to adopt the technology. James Cameron – long an advocate for emerging technologies in film-making – is on the board of a gen AI firm , citing his interest in how AI will intersect with CGI; Steven Soderbergh used Meta-powered tech to create animations for his recent documentary about John Lennon ; even Christopher Nolan, while dismissing the idea that AI will replace humans as “nonsense”, conceded that it will create some useful “imaging tools”. The current canary in the coalmine however is the storyboard artist, whose work gen AI appears to have directly in its sights. Storyboard artists are the illustrators who draw the panels of images with notes and diagrams that map out scenes before they are filmed. Storyboards are used to work out how a film will look, and as a blueprint to communicate a director’s vision to cast and crew , and are one of the first steps in bringing a script off the page. Now they appear on the verge of replacement by programmes that use text prompts to create illustrations instead. Even an old-school diehard like Martin Scorsese has got on board; in June he announced a partnership with an AI firm whose text-to-image model he used in the storyboarding process for his next movie. stories.title: What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
stories.summary: The billionaire tech executive finds himself mired in a personal and national security scandal.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Published 9 November 2026

One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report.

Jensen Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the affair.

It said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Jensen Huang is committed to continuing to lead the company.

Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.

Who is Alice Huang?

Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event

US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown.

Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023.

The company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia said this was investigated and debunked.

However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips.

The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang.

It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing.

When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.

"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.

China has rejected the spying allegations.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China."

There were media reports in October that US President Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf.

On whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump told journalists: "No, I don't think so. I think he's [Jensen Huang] an honourable guy."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Jensen Huang.

In spring this year, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Jensen Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman.

Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Published 1 day ago

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 1 day ago

Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair Published 17 hours ago

Why does it matter?

Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire boss's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers.

Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero.

Jensen Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

The revelations may explain why Jensen Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China .

Who is Jensen Huang?

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and US President Donald Trump at the White House

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff.

He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Jensen Huang.

Trump said he spoke with Jensen Huang after reports emerged about Alice Huang and her alledged links to the Chinese state and asked him: "'Did you have any idea she was a spy?

"He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," said Trump.

What investigations are now under way?

Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into the affair and has hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

It will be led by Joon Kim, a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District who is now at litigation partner at the law firm.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI was also investigating the affair . The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC.

Jensen Huang has also been asked to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees on 18 November.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee asked the Nvidia chief executive to appear to explain his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

Jensen Huang has yet to say he will comply, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC.

What is Nvidia and how important is it?

There is no clear successor for Jensen Huang at Nvidia

Founded by Jensen Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates .

Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch.

Huang bet on AI at a time when "there were no customers for the stuff he was building", Witt told the BBC.

Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure like Amazon, Google and Microsoft now use Nvidia chips.

Currently worth about $4tn, Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world.

For now, the firm's board appears unlikely to remove Jensen Huang, saying on Sunday they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".

Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake.

There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy.

His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles.

Who is Jensen Huang's wife?

Lori Huang and her husband at a state dinner by Trump for his Chinese President Xi Jinping

Jensen Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners.

They married in 1985 and have two children, Madison and Spencer.

In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.

Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

stories.summary: The 2026 US midterms set a record for campaign spending in a congressional election. According to OpenSecrets, a Washington-based non-profit organisation that tracks and publishes data on US campaign financing and lobbying, the Democratic and Republican parties are estimated to have spent nearly US$12 billion (£8.9 billion) between them. Both parties spend more in total on campaigning in presidential election years, as the chart below shows. But the latest figures represent a 26% increase in spending on congressional races compared with 2024. The Democrats accounted for 46% of the total amount spent in 2026, with 43% attributed to the Republicans. Independent candidates accounted for the other 11%. stories.body:
The 2026 US midterms set a record for campaign spending in a congressional election. According to OpenSecrets, a Washington-based non-profit organisation that tracks and publishes data on US campaign financing and lobbying, the Democratic and Republican parties are estimated to have spent nearly US$12 billion (£8.9 billion) between them.

Both parties spend more in total on campaigning in presidential election years, as the chart below shows. But the latest figures represent a 26% increase in spending on congressional races compared with 2024. The Democrats accounted for 46% of the total amount spent in 2026, with 43% attributed to the Republicans. Independent candidates accounted for the other 11%.

OpenSecrets data shows that “plutocrats”, a term used to describe people who hold social and political influence due to their wealth, largely back the Republicans. Democrat campaign spending, meanwhile, relies more heavily on smaller donations from large numbers of supporters.

In the run-up to the 2024 US presidential election, for example, the top five campaign donors gave just over US$863 million to the Republicans. Elon Musk was number one, with a donation of almost US$292 million for the Republicans and nothing for the Democrats.

Spending on US election campaigns (1998-2024)

Mike Bloomberg, a US businessman and the former three-term mayor of New York, was the most generous donor to the Democrats in the same cycle. He donated nearly US$61 million to the party, while giving US$1 million to the Republicans.

The final spending data for 2026 is yet to be published. But this trend looks to have continued. According to the BBC, Musk made the largest donation of the contest, spending almost US$450 million in support of Republican candidates.

By European standards, the spending on US election campaigns is enormous. Total spending on the UK’s 2024 general election was £94.5 million , a figure dwarfed by Musk’s contributions to the Republicans. But does election spending have any real effect?

Does campaign spending win votes?

The scale of the defeat for the Republicans in the 2026 midterms was unusual. Democrats took control of Congress and made gains in states that have been Republican for decades, including Kansas and Texas.

This raises the question of whether it was discontent with Donald Trump’s second term and the Republican Congress, as opposed to campaigning by the Democrats, that had more effect on the result.

A study from 2017 by American political scientists Joshua Kalla and David Broockman sheds light on this debate. They reviewed 49 different field experiments on the effects of election campaigning in the US and concluded that “the effects of campaign contact and advertising on Americans’ candidate choices in general elections is zero”.

They attributed much of this to partisanship, or the psychological attachment American voters have to political parties. This tends to override campaign messaging. If a voter is a strong Democrat, for example, they will probably ignore campaign messages from Republican candidates.

Other research has also found evidence that the saturation of political messaging during campaigns can turn people off politics in general, not just specific elections. Researchers call this effect “media malaise” .

Kalla and Broockman revised their conclusions slightly in 2023. Reporting the results of another experiment , they suggested there are “learning effects” in political campaigns – particularly for people who do not follow politics.

Voters may acquire information through campaigns that could affect their vote, such as finding out a particular candidate has been involved in a scandal.

But while acknowledging this can produce changes to the overall vote, they concluded that campaigning still has a relatively small impact on US election results.

These findings are consistent with other research, including the media malaise hypothesis. There is a consensus in the academic literature on the weak impact of campaign spending on US elections.

Campaign spending and House seats won by Republicans (1998-2024)

The second chart shows the relationship between campaign spending by the Republicans and the number of seats they won in the House of Representatives in the 13 US elections that took place between 1998 and 2024. It provides a rough guide to the effects of campaign spending in congressional elections.

The conclusion is that overall spending on campaigns has no significant effect on the results. This is consistent with the work of Kalla and Broockman and others, and raises the question of why Americans spend so much on their elections if doing so has such little effect.

The answer is that electoral competition shares characteristics with an arms race, where behaviour is driven largely by a fear of missing out. Candidates become anxious they will lose elections if their opponent campaigns and they do not.

This is much like the nuclear arms race in the 1950s and 1960s, in which the US and Soviet Union overinvested in nuclear weapons to the point that they could destroy each other many times over.

Campaign spending is not a complete waste of money. Many voters like to see the candidates they are voting for, while campaign work by candidates is expected by party activists. But the evidence shows that greater and greater spending has little effect on how people vote.

The lesson here is that it is easy to overstate the influence of plutocrats on electoral processes. When the new US Congress takes office in January 2027, one of its first acts should be to curb the expense associated with these campaigns.

stories.body:
Ice baths have become one of the most popular recovery strategies in sport. They are used by elite athletes and recreational gym-goers to reduce soreness and recuperate more quickly after exercising.

It has often been claimed that ice baths help to reduce pain and repair the muscle damage that intense exercise can cause. Yet when we look at the evidence, it isn’t clear that ice baths really are the best way to recover post exercise.

In a recent study , my colleagues and I compared ice baths against heat-based recovery methods. What we found suggests recovery is far more complex than simply cooling things down.

Muscle repair

Strenuous or unfamiliar exercise can cause damage to our muscle fibres. This is particularly the case after doing “eccentric exercises” , where muscles lengthen while generating force. Activities such as downhill running, descending the stairs or lowering a weight under control (while doing a barbell squat for instance) are all examples of eccentric exercise.

This exercise-induced muscle damage can leave your muscles feeling sore and weak. To repair the damage, the body triggers what’s known as an “inflammatory repair response” , where immune cells move into the muscle tissue to clear away damaged cellular material and stimulate regeneration.

Other molecules are also released to help coordinate repair . However, these molecules can also increase the sensitivity of pain receptors , which may further contribute to the muscle soreness that people experience up to 72 hours after an intense workout.

These responses are an important part of how the body repairs itself and becomes stronger.

We wanted to better understand what effect different recovery methods had on this repair process after a strenuous workout. So we recruited 40 healthy, physically active adults (31 men and nine women) and asked them to complete a specific exercise.

This involved repeatedly targeting the quadriceps – the large muscles at the front of the thigh – using a specialised machine that allowed us to carefully control the movement and measure muscle strength. This particular movement is known to cause temporary muscle damage and soreness – making it useful for studying how different recovery methods influence the body’s repair process.

Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four recovery methods: cold-water immersion (in water that was 10°C), hot-water immersion (in water that was 42°C), hot air exposure (60°C, similar to a sauna) and “passive recovery” which involved sitting and doing nothing for 30 minutes. Each method was carried out immediately after the workout.

Over the following 72 hours, we monitored recovery by looking at several measures – including muscle strength, pain and soreness, alongside various biological markers linked to muscle damage, inflammation and cellular stress.

All participants showed the expected signs of exercise-induced muscle damage. Strength declined immediately after exercise and soreness increased.

But when we looked at the effects of the recovery techniques, we were surprised to find that none of them restored muscle strength significantly faster than the others.

If strength had been the only outcome measured, we might have concluded the recovery methods made little difference. But the physiological data told a different story.

Participants who completed hot-water immersion were shown to have higher levels of a substance called “heat shock protein 72” (HSP72) which acts as a cellular maintenance and protection system , supporting repair processes and protecting cells during periods of physiological stress. It’s widely believed that HSP72 plays an important role in recovery and adaptation following exercise.

The heat-based recovery methods were also associated with more favourable changes in biological markers linked to muscle damage and inflammation.

So our findings suggest that exposure to heat may be better at stimulating the biological processes involved in recovery.

Cold-water immersion was not shown to improve any of the recovery markers measured in the study. It also showed the slowest recovery, with strength returning to around 82% of pre-exercise levels after 72 hours, compared with 88-89% in the other groups.

But cold-water immersion appeared more effective at reducing perceptions of muscle soreness. This highlights how feeling recovered and actually being physiologically recovered are not always the same thing.

These findings should be interpreted with some caution, however. The study involved 40 healthy, physically active adults – with just ten participants in each intervention group. While the study was adjusted to detect moderate effects, the sample size wasn’t large enough to explore potential differences between men and women.

The best way to recover

One of the most important lessons from our study is that recovery cannot be measured using a single outcome.

A person may feel less sore but may still have reduced muscle function. Also, important repair processes may be occurring inside the body without producing immediate improvements in performance.

This distinction may help explain why recovery research has produced mixed findings over the years. Different interventions may influence different aspects of recovery.

Read more: The workout recovery techniques backed by science – and the ones that are just hype

If your priority is reducing how sore you feel after a workout, cold-water immersion may be the most beneficial. But if your goal is to influence the biological processes that help your muscles to repair and adapt, heat-based recovery may be a better choice.

Our findings don’t suggest that ice baths are completely ineffective. Ice baths were still found to help people feel better.

What our study shows is that recovery is about far more than how you feel the next day. Sometimes the most important changes are happening beneath the surface.
