This video can not be played

Listen: Berry tells Cash about his invitation to meet a senior Chinese official

Berry tells Cash he was driven to a government-owned villa in a grand compound.

The experience "felt like a psychological game of chess" and "like a test", Berry says.

He kept his hands under the table as tea was served: "I didn't want it to be obvious if I was nervous. I tested to see if my hands were shaking first, then drank the tea."

Berry describes the senior Chinese official asking via an interpreter "about the situation in the UK at the moment, about the Tory leadership thing".

At that time, Boris Johnson had just resigned as the UK's prime minister, and a Conservative leadership battle was taking place, which Liz Truss would go on to win.

Berry says he jokingly tried to ask his host which candidate China wanted, but the interpreter did not translate his question.

"And then the main guy just shakes my hand like it's time to go," Berry tells Cash.

After receiving the voice notes, Cash replies via text the next day: "You, my friend, have just been elite captured" before adding: "You're in spy territory now".

In many media reports these particular messages, previously released in a government witness statement, have been presented as a smoking gun - evidence that Cash knew his friend was passing on information to the Chinese state.

But Cash insists it was a "tongue-in-cheek joke" because he knew his friend to be "a staunch critic of the Chinese Communist Party".

The next morning, he made a joke about Berry spying for the UK and getting in trouble with the Chinese authorities, he says. Cash texted: "Keep him sweet… We may have a use for you yet".

"I didn't believe he was knowingly spying on the UK through me," says Cash. "I trusted my friend… I wish I had seen the danger earlier, spotted it and cut off all contact."

'Bigger deal than I thought'

So who was the mystery official Berry had met?

"I found out who this guy is," Berry text-messaged Cash a few hours later. "Bigger deal than I thought."

Berry posted a link to the Wikipedia page of Cai Qi, who at the time was one of China's most influential politicians and is now, in effect, President Xi Jinping's chief of staff.

Berry identified Cai Qi (left) as the man he had met - a trusted aide of Chinese President Xi Jinping

Whether Berry correctly identified his host remains unclear. He has since disputed the suggestion that he met someone as senior as Cai Qi.

What is beyond dispute is that he believed he may have met someone highly placed within the Chinese political system.

For Chris Cash, this unusual encounter did not prompt alarm bells. Asked why not, Cash tells the BBC: "Because I didn't think anything of the meeting, really."

We ask Cash why his friend might have been asked to such a meeting. "Strange things happen in China... you know we would often brush shoulders with sort of quite senior members of the Chinese communist party," he tells us.

Challenged about whether he had read the Wikipedia link at the time, Cash says he had "skimmed it", adding that it described him as a judge and a provincial-level official. "I just thought it was a weird meeting with a guy who'd taken an interest," he says.

Six months later, Berry said in text messages that "off the record" he had it "on pretty good authority" that China was considering dropping sanctions against Tom Tugendhat, one of the Conservative MPs in the China Research Group, where Cash worked.

Berry wrote that this would happen as long as the West "continued to show signals that they are willing to work together".

The Chinese believed it would be "extremely embarrassing" if Tugendhat became prime minister or foreign secretary while under Chinese sanctions, Berry said.

At the time of the meeting in summer 2022, China-sceptic Tugendhat was seen as a possible contender to succeed Boris Johnson, or become UK foreign secretary.

He was actually appointed as security minister by Liz Truss, and Beijing lifted sanctions on him in January 2026.

Was Cash concerned that Berry appeared to be passing information to him about Chinese foreign policy?

Cash says he assumed Berry had heard this "through the grapevine at his company" which was doing business with the UK.

He says he never doubted his friend's trustworthiness, to the extent he even named Berry as a reference on his application for a security pass for the Palace of Westminster.

The pass was granted and, a fortnight before their arrests in early 2023, Cash invited Berry to Parliament for lunch.

It was to be their final face-to-face conversation.

'Complete shock'

Cash was in bed at quarter to six on a March morning when he was woken by car doors being shut, he says. Within seconds, four UK counter-terrorism officers had barged into his bedroom at his parents' home in Edinburgh.

"They told me to sit up and not touch anything and then said I was under arrest for breaching the Official Secrets Act," Cash says.

"I was in complete shock… quivering... My mum was hysterical."

Cash says the officers dressed him in dirty clothes he had worn that weekend, handcuffed him and marched him down to an unmarked police car. He was later driven to London.

Chris Berry was also arrested the same day.

It remains unclear how, when and why British security services became interested in the exchanges between the two friends.

But they are likely to have found out far more about their relationship when Berry was stopped and questioned by counter-terror officers at Heathrow Airport.

His laptop and phone were taken - this may have enabled his Signal chats to be downloaded.

Berry later messaged Cash about it.

Cash says he had not been alarmed by this: "I thought it was just standard... for a guy who'd been in China."

As the investigation progressed, it became clear the authorities believed Cash and Berry had been involved in an informal, but dangerous, exchange of information that was "prejudicial to the safety and interests of the UK".

The allegations were based on 6,273 messages between the pair - the same ones Cash has now shared with the BBC. Cash's solicitor has told the BBC they are genuine.

They cover a period when Cash had joined the China Research Group (CRG), founded by Tugendhat and fellow Tory MP Alicia Kearns, and when Berry was working for a Chinese company called Strong, where part of his work involved writing political and economic reports for clients.

According to court documents, Berry was said to have compiled 34 reports for a man linked to the Chinese state spy agency, relaying information passed on to him by Cash. Strong did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

The CRG's office was across the Thames from Westminster, but Cash regularly had meetings in Parliament. Cash did not have government security clearance and there is no evidence he had access to classified documents.

Despite being thousands of miles apart, the two friends remained in close contact, often messaging daily.

The messages reviewed by the BBC show them discussing topics including sanctions on China, the tech company Huawei, human rights, Hong Kong, Taiwan and British foreign policy.

Cash says he used the Signal app for almost all his contacts with people in China - "more for their protection" - as he says discussing the government "could land someone… in trouble". He and Berry did not use the app's "disappearing messages" function.

Much of the information they discussed was publicly available, says Cash - who has given the BBC a detailed spreadsheet with links and references in an attempt to prove it.

But sometimes he did share with Berry his impressions from meetings and private discussions in Westminster. On 12 occasions in the messages, he labelled information "off the record" or "very off the record" before passing it on.

Cash says this was "just me excitedly sharing things that I was doing with him at work".

One message recounted views allegedly expressed in private by Britain's then-ambassador to China, Dame Caroline Wilson, during a discussion with the CRG about its work on China's influence on UK universities.

Cash also messaged Berry sharing unverified rumours about the sex lives of two UK cabinet ministers. There is no evidence Berry passed this to his Chinese colleagues.

Cash says he regarded such exchanges as routine political discussion. "We weren't working with classified information," he says.

Acquitted and 'traduced'

Cash was told by his solicitor the police investigation would blow over after six months and he would soon be able to return to normal life.

But in September 2023 - six months after the arrests - the case became public when the Sunday Times broke the story of an unnamed "spy" who had been arrested in Parliament.

Cash recalls travelling on a train while, around him, fellow passengers read the newspaper's front page story: "Commons 'Chinese spy' arrested". He says: "I wanted the world to eat me up."

Within 24 hours he was named and pictured in the press, and both men were later charged with espionage.

In September the following year, just weeks before their trial was due to begin, Cash received an unexpected call from his solicitor.

"Are you sitting down?" he asked Cash. "They've dropped all the charges."

His lawyers requested a court hearing for the prosecution to formally acknowledge that they would offer no evidence, but at the Old Bailey the newly-innocent Cash struggled to find anyone interested in his story.

Cash's life has changed almost beyond recognition, he says, but he is positive about the future

At every previous court appearance he had been mobbed, but the press had not been informed about this hearing.

Eventually his team found a lone BBC journalist. "I said my piece outside the Old Bailey. And that was a real high point. I felt that I could start to move on with my life."

It wouldn't be that simple.

Across the city, House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle was seething. "It is this Parliament that has been spied on," he declared. "It is MPs' offices that have been infiltrated."

There would be days of political debate and a raucous prime minister's questions where Tory leader Kemi Badenoch would claim: "This all stinks of a cover-up."

"I'd been acquitted by law, but then I was traduced in Parliament," Cash says. "It was almost like I was convicted in the court of public opinion again, by people who I had worked with and trusted and that felt horrible."

Today Cash's life is almost unrecognisable. He has lost his dream job, his relationship, and his closest friend from university.

"We talked about being each other's best men," Cash says. Instead, when the friend got married last year, Cash was not even invited.

He is also no longer in contact with Berry.

"I've been applying for basic admin jobs and having trouble recently," Cash says.

"I'm angry and upset with how everything played out, and I do feel let down."

But when asked, Cash stops short of saying he feels Berry betrayed him. Does he think his friend was spying for the Chinese government?

"He would have to have his time in court to defend himself," Cash answers. "I think it'd be wrong of me to speculate and hypocritical given the speculation that I've been subject to. But we're no longer friends."

Berry declined to comment on this story, but at the time of his acquittal said his reports "concerned economic and commercial issues widely discussed in the UK at the time and drew on information freely in the public domain".

Like his former friend, Chris Cash is innocent in the eyes of the law, but his reputation has undoubtedly been trashed.

Many in Parliament still think they were spies. And with more of the messages between these former friends now revealed, the debate over their actions could be reignited.

"It was a gruelling ordeal," Cash says. "But I'm a fundamentally positive person… I'm positive about what the future holds."

The AI chip boss’s actions raise urgent questions about corporate influence, national security and the US president’s willingness to listen to intelligence warnings

I t could be the plot of a spy thriller. One of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswomen said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. When Donald Trump was briefed about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s liaisons with Alice Huang, he took no action. Perhaps he thought only marriage vows had been broken. Or perhaps Mr Trump was willing to overlook the conduct of a friend who championed his unpopular datacentre expansion, whose company donated to his White House ballroom and who echoed his opposition to AI safeguards against expert advice.

Nvidia became the cornerstone of AI by supplying brute computing power. As tech giants scrambled for the firm’s graphics processing units (GPUs), Mr Huang sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush – and amassed a $160bn fortune. When China joined the race for tech supremacy, Nvidia’s microchips became a national security issue. In October 2022, the US slapped export controls on GPU sales to China. Thirty months later, Nvidia was effectively banned from selling to Beijing. Mr Huang lobbied for looser controls. Such was his sway with Mr Trump that the White House scrapped Biden-era global AI chip restrictions and then permitted sales of Nvidia’s prized H200 processors to Chinese customers.

Democrats, buoyed by their midterms’ success, will be looking for answers. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence, the president replied: “ No, I don’t think so. ” That makes the question of his reasons unavoidable. There could be trouble at Mr Trump’s commerce department if it backed Mr Huang’s policy agenda and loosened export controls despite knowing of his affair with a Chinese spy. Reports suggest that the commerce department’s probe was halted after Nvidia called investigators. Congress clearly has grounds to investigate whether the Trump administration knowingly disregarded a foreign intelligence threat. Whatever happens next, Mr Huang’s admission is likely to be the beginning, not the end, of the saga.

Rumours had swirled for months that Nvidia’s boss had been in a “ special relationship ” with Ms Huang – an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that in 2025 was revealed to be under investigation for suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China. What makes this extraordinary is the possibility that Mr Huang’s romantic and commercial relationship exposed him to a Chinese intelligence operation. In May, analysts at Culper Research argued that Megaspeed brought Nvidia substantial revenues, allegedly backed by Chinese financing. Then Nividia’s boss publicly defended Megaspeed while secretly conducting an affair with its top executive. More than $300bn was wiped off Nvidia’s valuation as soon as Wall Street opened.

Industrial espionage is nothing new. Richer nations often block the export of their commercial secrets to prevent others from catching up . These challengers often go to extraordinary lengths to obtain new technology. Historically, diplomatic or military so-called honeytraps – spies sent to seduce victims to gain confidential information – have been more common than commercial ones. But in 2008, British spy agencies accused Beijing of a campaign to target businesses, using sex to pressure targets into cooperating. Whether that has happened here is unknown. But a president who promised to get tough on China needs to explain why his administration eased chip export controls despite warnings that the businessman lobbying for it might be compromised.

stories.body:
Jens Eskelund says Europe may need to allow its companies to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains

Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese counterparts by the end of the decade if current trends continue amid fears over mass job losses, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China has warned.

In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.

Eskelund, who heads the influential Beijing-headquartered body, said European manufacturers could find themselves at an existential crossroads by the end of the decade, asking themselves: “What is the point of trading?”

As the EU gets tough with China with a deficit running at a record £1bn (€1.18bn) a day and an increasing mood for protectionism in Brussels, Berlin and Paris, he said European countries might need to shift their policies to allow domestic manufacturers to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains, rather than treat them as competitors.

Eskelund, who is also a managing director of the shipping group Maersk’s Chinese operations, pointed to a report by Goldman Sachs that forecasted Chinese exports would lower the EU’s gross domestic product by 0.5% by the end of the decade while reducing Germany’s by up to 0.9%.

“It raises the question, if China’s trade delivers negative value, why trade?” the Danish businessman said.

“If you are suddenly in a situation where trade creates a lot of value for one party, but it destroys value for the other, countries will begin to ask themselves, why do we trade?” he said, pointing to a potential doomsday scenario in which manufacturing disappeared from European countries, causing mass job losses, collapse in the tax base and potential multigenerational unemployment and spiralling social benefits costs.

Speaking in Brussels, where he has been in back-to-back meetings with European Commission officials to give them feedback from Beijing, he said Europe is at an inflection point.

“If we create new dependencies, ultimately that might result in Europe losing its ability to determine its own future,” with mass job losses and fraying of communities, Eskelund added.

That existential threat is already beginning to bite in Europe’s car, chemicals and renewable energy sectors, with the German automotive industry hit by a double whammy of reduced profits in China and cheap competition at home from Chinese companies such as BYD, Geely and SAIC Motor. Last week, BMW said its sales in China had dropped 22% in the first nine months of the year, in line with expectations of suppressed domestic demand, while issuing a second profit warning this year.

Eskelund is not a fan of the term “China shock 2.0” – which refers to the impact of the huge rise in exports of, cars, chemicals and components – on local industry to the EU in the last five years. He said it should not have come as a surprise as Beijing’s plans to displace imports were the enduring theme of the last three five-year plans since Beijing’s Made in China strategy was agreed in 2015.

“I don’t really like the term China shock 2.0 because these things that are happening should not be a shock because it is all written in their five-year plans so you should be able to anticipate that,” Eskelund said.

“The proof of concept here is that China has been laser-focused on reducing its own dependencies over the last 30 years,” he added, pointing to a concomitant reduction in imports.

A recent report by Centre for European Reform (CER) urged Germany to stop “admiring” Beijing and change its strategy, with China’s latest five-year plan (2026 to 2030) a doubling-down on “self-reliance”.

“It is committed to displacing imports in the few sectors where it still depends on foreign supply,” said the CER.

The sectors that have been identified in China’s latest five-year plan are AI, quantum computing; robotics; smart and green tech; biomanufacturing; brain-computer interfaces ; and 6G communications.

Solar panels, wind turbines, robots, driverless cars, advanced chips are part of China’s new strategy for global domination.

Eskelund’s advice to those industries in Europe is not to hide but brace themselves for China to deliver. Once a strategy is decided in Beijing, incentives, tax breaksand subsidies flow down by region to town and village levels. Officials across the country know what to focus on and do, he said.

after newsletter promotion

His advice to EU leaders: “Engage with China and discuss getting to a point where everyone can see value is being created for both sides”, something he thinks Beijing understands.

While this might be an obvious point, Eskelund said a fundamental shift in approach was needed in Europe.

“China has always been very focused on outcomes, whereas Europe has been more focused on principles. It raises the question of whether following principles is delivering undesirable outcomes,” Eskelund said.

A view expressed in some quarters, including the UK, that trade imbalance could be addressed by increasing exports was just “fantasy”, said Eskelund, with this year’s surplus against the rest of the world expected to surpass 2025’s record $1.2tn (£900bn).

Eskelund said many companies were still making good money in China but the brutal competition in the country’s supply chains, combined with a currency undervalued by about 30%, left Europeans in the dust.

“What we see right now is that in almost all industrial verticals, almost anywhere in the world, you would have one and probably several Chinese competitors” he said.

“It’s just very, very difficult in most industries to compete with the Chinese.”

Giving up on trade is not the answer. If you can’t beat them join them. And that is what is now happening, the chamber has found.

“One way that they can compete with the Chinese supply chain is to become a part of the Chinese supply chain itself,” Eskelund said.

“For many companies it’s not the profit that you make in China that matters as much as the way Chinese supply chains enable you to compete on a global marketplace.”

This could mean making the products in China in joint domestic partnerships with European companies and getting into global supply chains in conjunction with Chinese firms.

“It is a sort of evolution from the old days when you came to China to service the Chinese market in China for China. It has now become: be in China, for the world. I think it’s a fairly significant shift,” Eskelund said.

For many of his members this had led to an “uptick in confidence” in the past year.

“This has turned out to be one of the ways that companies adapt, faced with a saturated market in China, they begin to explore exports,” he said.

Exclusive: Iran war has fuelled energy price rise and clouded outlook, driving up unemployment, says Clare Lombardelli

Young people in Britain are bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” as employers hold back from hiring amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East, a deputy governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Clare Lombardelli, the Bank’s deputy governor for monetary policy, said the unfolding conflict, which has triggered a surge in energy prices and clouded the outlook for the economy, was contributing to an increase in youth unemployment.

“What you see is the cost falling on young people, so you can see this rapid rise in the number of young people who are struggling to find jobs,” she said.

Against a highly volatile backdrop, she also warned Threadneedle Street was preparing for a “live” decision on interest rates next month after it increased the cost of borrowing last week for the first time in three years .

In an interview with the Guardian, Lombardelli said the UK’s employers were attempting to navigate the complex geopolitical backdrop by holding on to staff and freezing new recruitment.

“It’s what I call a low-gear economy. So a labour market where you’re seeing a real fall-off in hiring. But actually, we’re not seeing much in the way of redundancies. What’s going on is this kind of low hire, low fire dynamic,” she said.

“They [employers] are delaying hiring. They want to see if this uncertainty is going to resolve – like all of us. None of us thought we’d be nine months into this conflict.

“If firms are not hiring, obviously, by definition, that means people that are new to the labour market are hurt by that.”

Her comments come as Andy Burnham’s government awaits the findings of a report into young people and work by the former Labour cabinet minister, Alan Milburn, which is expected to be published next week.

With employers facing rising costs triggered by the Iran war, higher taxes and weaker levels of demand from consumers squeezed by the cost of living crisis, unemployment in the UK has risen this year to 4.7% . Youth unemployment has risen at a sharper rate to the highest levels outside the Covid pandemic since 2015.

Tackling the UK’s youth jobs crisis is also a growing priority for the government after an increase in the number of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.

Lombardelli is expected to outline her concerns over a slowdown in labour market dynamism at a speech in London on Tuesday.

Lombardelli joined the majority of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) in voting to lift the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. She said a further quarter-point rise could be warranted from as early as its next policy meeting in December.

“Every meeting is live for us. December is, you know, it’s certainly plausible. What’s the market pricing at the moment? It’s about 50/50 for December,” she said.

after newsletter promotion

“I think it depends what we see on the conflict and the energy prices and it depends what we see in the wider data and how all that fits together. But I wouldn’t rule it out. Equally, I don’t have enough information just yet.”

Lombardelli was among members of the MPC who joined the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, in raising the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, after the Democrats’ victories in the US Congress, which some investors have interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump said at the weekend that he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progressed.

Lombardelli, a former Treasury and OECD economist, said the impact of an increasingly stagnant jobs market was being seen particularly in sectors that offer young people their first job. “So that might be hospitality, it might be retail, in particular,” she said. “If you look at the distribution of where variances are, they’ve really fallen off in those sectors where young people can get their first start in the labour market.”

She added that employers surveyed by the Bank suggested there is “a sense that hiring a young person is a higher risk than it used to be”.

Threadneedle Street is focusing heavily on the jobs market amid concerns that current high levels of inflation could become entrenched in the economy if workers have enough bargaining power to push for higher wage settlements – which could lead companies to put up their prices to cover higher wage bills, stoking inflation. Signs of a weaker labour market could diminish this risk.

However, Lombardelli said that higher levels of unemployment would not necessarily bear down on inflationary pressures. This is because employers – holding on to the staff they needed – were only hiring for positions they found harder to fill.

“You can have higher unemployment without it exerting a downward pressure on inflation,” she said. “So that’s obviously a problem.”

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boom

Published 10 November 2026

Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe .

The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.

Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.

It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.

Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.

Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.

Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy Published 8 hours ago

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 1 day ago

According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him.

However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.

The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary.

When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.

Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts.

The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company.

He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.

It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang.

A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

Introduction: Nvidia, down $430bn, hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.

The crisis gripping Nvidia is gathering pace, with around $430bn wiped off the value of the world’s most valuable company since it was hit by a spying scandal.

Overnight, Nvidia announced it has hired a former top federal prosecutor to help probe chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company’s board have retained Joon H. Kim , the former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York, and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct “a thorough and independent investigation”.

Wachtell is a heavyweight corporate law firm. In 2022 it was hired by Twitter to force Elon Musk to complete his $44bn takeover, for example, and has a track record of advising major companies on issues such as mergers and corporate governance.

It will now look into the circumstances of Huang’s affair – thought to be with Alice Huang , who US officials believe is a Chinese spy, and who worked for Nvidia customer Megaspeed.

Although Beijing has denied allegations that it operated an espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s value has been buffeted this week.

Yesterday, its shares fell by almost 5.5%, adding to the 4.27% drop on Monday. This has pulled the company’s value down to $4.07tn, from $4.50tn before the story broke last weekend.

The agenda

9.45am BST: ECB President Lagarde taking part on panel discussion at 9th Paris Peace Forum in Paris

Noon BST: US weekly mortgage approvals data

2.15pm GMT: Chancellor John Healey quizzed by Treasury committee on the budget

Ending the conflict in the Middle East would be the single best economic policy for Britain, John Healey tells the Treasury committee.

The chancellor explains:

double quotation mark I went into this budget process less than four months ago, with really deep concerns about the global economic storms that we faced, which had not been reflected in the OBR spring forecast. And now the OBR and the Bank of England are really clear – The conflict in the Middle East is driving rising energy costs, driving debt, increased costs, and it’s also weakening economic growth that’s hitting nations worldwide. But it’s hitting us particularly hard in this country.

Chancellor Healey also told MPs that “I am ready to say no to data centres” if they don’t have community benefits.

He says he does not want to see a “free-for-all on data centres as we saw in the US”... but equally says pushing to win investment in AI and that development of the sector is “inevitable”.

John Healey has also revealed that UK AI chip startup Fractile has been valued at $7bn in its latest fundraising round.

The chancellor told MP that Fractile has just conducted a £500m funding round, including a contribution from the British Business Bank.

This lifted the valuation of this “British based company, British started company to $7 billion”, through the “largest ever European semiconductor funding round”, Healey adds proudly.

Fractile is developing chips designed to improve AI inference, the process through which AI models generate responses.

Tech shares are broadly higher on Wall Street in early trading, lifting the Nasdaq Composite index up by 1.2%.

CoreWeave is leading the risers, up 12%, after cheering investors with its financial results last night.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, says the AI trade is turning a corner:

double quotation mark The roller coaster ride for markets continues, and US stocks are staging a recovery today, after Tuesday’s post CPI sell off. US stocks are surging, led by Nvidia is higher by more than 2.5% so fa

Back in the tech world, Nvidia’s shares have opened higher.

After two days of falls, Nvidia’s share price is up 2% in early trading.

John Healey 'dismayed' by budget bank tax leak

Chancellor John Healey says he is “dismayed” that the details of his bank tax plans leaked on the morning of the budget.

He tells the Treasury committee that he did not want any leaks out of the budget process, and takes all leaks seriously.

Healey says he was determined as chancellor to avoid budget leaks, after seeing the damage caused by the flurry of reports ahead of the budget in 2025.

The chancellor explains:

double quotation mark There are real world impacts, not just moving the markets or the gilt yields. We saw last year with speculation, kite flying, leaks, briefings. We saw people cashing in their pension pots, where they didn’t need to. We saw people cancelling and changing investment plans when they didn’t need to.

MPs grill Treasury over bank tax leak

Over in parliament, MPs are grilling top brass from the Treasury about last month’s budget – starting with the leak of the chancellor’s bank tax plans.

Q: Was this the worst type of breach you can think of?

James Bowler, permanent secretary at the HM Treasury, says it is “deeply regrettable and frustrating” that Bloomberg had “the shape” of the bank tax on the morning of the budget, before it was announced that afternoon.

[Reminder: Bloomberg reported that the surcharge would only rise by 3 percentage points, and would be temporary]

But no, he argues it is not the worst type – it doesn’t compare to the situation last year, he argues.

Q: but was the leak an example of inside information?

Bowler replies that the market did move after the report (bank shares went up).

Chancellor John Healey steps in too, promising that the results of the investigation into the leak will be shared with this committee .

Europe’s largest energy grid operator E.ON ⁠is reviewing whether former nuclear plant sites in Germany ⁠could be ⁠converted ​into data centres.

Finance chief Nadia Jakobi told analysts today:

double quotation mark “These former power plants can provide attractive industrial locations and ‌depending on the site, we can use the existing infrastructure, ​particularly the large grid connection.

She added that E.ON is taking a “first step” with ⁠US chip designer Nvidia .

Taylor Wimpey cuts homebuilding forecast again

Taylor Wimpey, one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders, has cut its outlook for home completions for a second time this year and blamed rising mortgage and living costs – another sign of a weakening housing market.

The government’s 1.5m new homes target over five years looks even more out of reach, as the company joined others in warning of a “subdued” autumn selling season. It comes after Britain’s biggest brickmaker, Ibstock, issued a profit warning last week.

Taylor ‌Wimpey now expects to complete 10,500 homes this year, excluding joint ventures, ‌below its previous forecast of 10,600 to 10,800 homes. Adjusted operating profit is expected to be at the lower end of its £262m to £299m range. The firm also reduced its outlook in July.

Its order book declined to 6,839 homes as of 8 November, versus 7,253 a year earlier. Taylor Wimpey has also been hit by higher build cost inflation, running at 3% to 4%, due to knock-on effects from the Iran war.

Jennie Daly , the chief executive, said:

double quotation mark “The autumn selling season has been more subdued, as higher mortgage rates and living costs continue to reduce customer affordability.”

Its share price fell 4.5% in early trading and is now 3.5% lower, and dragged down rival Persimmon, which is trading 1% lower.

The Bank of England raised its base rate last week, from 3.75% to 4%, which hit mortgage borrowers but will benefit savers. The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, said another hike could be needed soon, but this (partly) depends on a resolution of the Iran war and the consequent impact on energy prices and inflation.

To entice buyers, Taylor Wimpey is offering more incentives than usual, for example a deposit top-up and one-off mortgage contribution. And it has cut its selling prices by 2.5% year on year.

It said it is well positioned to participate in the government’s new Your First Home scheme aimed at first-time buyers. But the scheme won’t launch until April, and experts have warned that the market could remain sluggish until then.

Investment bank Baird has cut its rating on Nvidia’s shares to ‘neutral’, and slashed their target price for the stock, Reuters report.

Having previously predicted Nvidia could reach $500, Baird have lowered their target price to $200 (reminder, they closed at $168.89 last night).

The FT’s Unhedged column has a handy breakdown of what we know about the Nvidia crisis…

Nvidia is the indispensable supplier and, increasingly, financier of the infrastructure powering the entire AI boom;

Huang is the boom’s chief salesperson and its most influential figure who is not running one of the AI labs;

Huang is a trusted adviser to Donald Trump on the US-China AI race and AI regulation;

US intelligence has believed for months that Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang.

And some things we don’t know (but which Joon H. Kim may answer!):

Did Huang mislead Nvidia’s board? Did he disclose that he had a conflict of interest with a major and geopolitically sensitive customer?

Did the board know US intelligence suspected Alice Huang of being linked to Chinese intelligence?

Did the company know about the affair when it told The New York Times two weeks ago that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected” for the executive of an important commercial partner?

How strong is the evidence that has led US intelligence to conclude that Alice Huang is a spy

And the upshot is that removing Jensen Huang may simply be too big a risk, they suggest.

Although, as my colleague Nils Pratley wrote this week, Huang may look less powerful once the investigation has concluded…

Stocks in the AI sector are back in demand, after cloud computing provider Coreweave reported strong results last night.

Coreweave, which rents out computing clusters powered by Nvidia’s GPU chips, predicted it would hit profitability in 2028, easing some concerns over its financial health.

The cost of insuring CoreWeave’s debt against default has been rising in recent weeks, on concerns that AI demand might not be strong enought to support its borrowing.

Shares in CoreWeave are up 14.4% in premarket trading.

stories.title: Scottish Labour leader says the UK should re-join EU
stories.summary: Michael Marra said he wanted "solidarity, not separation" and accepted that "re-joining the EU won't be easy".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Michael Marra said getting back in the EU should be a "long-term objective"

Published 10 November 2026

The Scottish Labour leader has called for the UK to re-join the European Union, insisting it should be a "long-term objective" for the whole country.

During his first major speech since becoming party leader, Michael Marra said he wanted "solidarity, not separation" and accepted that "re-joining the EU won't be easy".

Marra acknowledged there would be "serious questions" over issues such as currency and borders before the UK could return to the EU.

Last month, the UK government ruled out re-joining the EU within this parliament but Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer ties with Europe.

The UK Labour leader suggested another referendum on the issue could feature in a future Labour manifesto.

Speaking at the University of Edinburgh, Marra said: "The UK should re-join the European Union and Scottish Labour will work to make that happen.

"I don't pretend it will happen quickly. But I believe we should set it as a long-term objective for the UK and that Scotland should lead the change in making that happen."

Andy Burnham will be travelling to Brussels next week where he is expected to sign a series of deals with the EU

Marra accepted his call goes further than Prime Minister Andy Burnham's position.

He added: "Re-joining the EU is not the current policy of the UK Labour Party and not the current policy of the UK government.

"The UK Labour Party isn't there yet. This is a distinct Scottish Labour position."

Marra's predecessor, Anas Sarwar, had pushed for closer ties with the EU after Brexit but did not go as far as to call for the UK to re-join the bloc.

"It is in Scotland's interests, and in the interests of the whole United Kingdom, for the UK to re-join the European Union," added Marra.

Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn't expect a smooth ride Published 3 days ago

UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC Published 4 days ago

Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again Published 13 October

Addressing party supporters, Marra set out how going back into Europe would boost the economy.

The North East MSP said that "breaking down barriers" with European nations would "help Scottish businesses grow, attract investment and create better-paid jobs".

It could also "help bring down prices and generate more money for our public services", he added.

Marra accepted that re-joining the EU "won't solve every problem we have", but added: "If we're serious about growth, we cannot keep ignoring the opportunity on our doorstep."

His speech came ahead of the prime minister travelling to Brussels next week where he is expected to sign a series of deals with the EU.

These will be focused on bringing down post-Brexit trade barriers on food and farming, as well as working more closely on emissions trading and making it easier for young people from the UK to work, live and study in Europe, and vice versa.

A 'roadmap back to Europe'

Responding to Marra's speech, SNP deputy leader Keith Brown said: "Having accepted that people are able to revisit the EU referendum decision taken 10 years ago, how can any Labour Party politician now seriously claim Scotland can't revisit the independence referendum decision taken 12 years ago?"

Marra told BBC Scotland News that he did not support a second referendum, and said he believed the people of Scotland did not either.

Scottish Liberal Democrats leader Alex Cole-Hamilton said he was pleased to see Scottish Labour following his party's lead.

He added: "It's important to offer the people of Britain a realistic roadmap back to Europe. That starts with re-joining the single market and establishing a customs union as a key first step."

The Scottish Greens' co-leader Gillian Mackay said she agrees with Marra that Scotland's "place is in the EU" - but added it was hypocritical to support this while ignoring "growing demand" for an Independence referendum.

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said people in Scotland were "sick of constant constitutional uncertainty" and want "politicians to focus on the cost-of-living, cutting taxes and fixing public service".

Reform UK Scotland's Max Bannerman said the country does not need to re-join the EU to see growth.

Analysis: Marra makes his move - but why now?

Michael Marra has set a very clear policy direction for his party. So why now?

Andy Burnham took the first step by taking his tin opener to this can of political worms at the Labour Party conference as he seeks closer ties with the EU.

There's a crunch summit in Brussels a week on Friday.

But Marra is going further than the prime minister.

He points out rejoining the EU is not the current policy of the UK government and that this is a distinct, Scottish Labour position.

Marra is a new leader and he needs to make the news with a stand-out position, so that also helps to answer the "why now" question.

Scottish Labour believe their leader has two clear roles; challenge the Scottish government and influence the UK government.

Marra thinks he can be influential and it's a change even from the position he held when he took over as leader.

There may be a fair amount of Scottish public support for this and brings Labour alongside the SNP as they both burnish their pro-EU credentials.

Labour and the SNP will continue their traditional battle and now Marra has a new fight on his hands to fully convince his party of his stance as he demands "rejoin" be included in their next general election manifesto.

stories.summary: Conservative shadow minister Helen Whately says the system risks putting children on a "conveyor belt" towards a "lifetime on benefits".

stories.body:
Published 10 November 2026

The Conservatives have pledged to save £2.8bn a year by ending Disability Living Allowance (DLA) payments to families of children with "milder cases" of behavioural disorders, learning difficulties or ADHD.

The policy is one of a series of measures which the party says will save £36bn from the welfare budget.

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the system risked putting children on a "conveyor belt" towards a "lifetime on benefits".

Labour described the Tories' plan as a "charter for homelessness and human misery that would push people into hardship and end up costing the state more".

DLA for children allows parents to claim between £30.30 and £194.60 per week to help cover the additional costs that come with raising a disabled child.

The child must either have difficulty getting about or need more looking after than a child of the same age who does not have a disability.

The Conservatives say child DLA is the "fastest growing benefit in the UK's welfare system", citing government statistics showing the number of cases had risen from 521,476 in 2020 to 914,000.

The party is proposing that in cases where a claim is for a behavioural disorder, learning difficulty or ADHD, only those with the highest need will be eligible for cash payments.

Under the party's plans, those with the most severe conditions, representing around 30% of cases, would continue to receive payments.

The remaining 70% would lose the money but instead receive support through mental health services and family hubs, into which the Conservatives have said they will invest £1bn.

The changes would apply to new claims and reassessments. Those with physical disabilities would be exempt.

The party's other previously-announced cuts include:

£13.7bn from changes to sickness and disability benefits including restricting payments to claimants with "milder mental health issues and neurodiversity conditions such as anxiety, depression and ADHD"

£9.5bn by making it harder for foreign nationals to claim benefits

£4.5bn by reducing local housing allowance payments

£3.1bn by reintroducing the two-child benefit cap

£1bn from tackling fraud

Setting out the party's plans, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities even when they face serious challenges.

"Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world.

"If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself."

What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending? Published 29 October

How a rise in ADHD benefits claims is adding to welfare spending challenge Published 9 July

'Worrying' number of teens lose disability benefits Published 12 March 2025

The Labour government has said it wants to bring the benefits bill down but has not set out a timetable for any reductions.

More details of its plans are expected to come after former minister Alan Milburn has published his review on young people not in education, employment and training.

Both Milburn's review and a review into disability benefits, co-chaired by Minister Sir Stephen Timms, will be published in November.

Asked about Milburn's review, Whately said he was "rolling the pitch for more welfare spending" adding: "We're in no question and no doubt that you can make savings from welfare - it's just that Labour doesn't want to do that."

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives designed and implemented this benefit system, which has driven large numbers of people to be signed off and written off.

"Labour is tackling the collapse in face-to-face assessments, bringing in personalised employment support for sick and disabled people and spreading opportunity to young people through the Youth Guarantee."

The Child Poverty Action Group said: "These proposals would take the UK back to the dark ages, causing the biggest overnight increase in child poverty since records began."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: "Until the Conservatives face up to the damage their botched Brexit deal has done, they will remain an out-of-touch, anti-growth, anti-business party, and it will be disabled people and children growing up in poverty who will pay the price."

Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision

For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large.

He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares.

But Huang’s image as a family man has been shattered as of Sunday. After the New York Times revealed at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset who he had developed a close relationship with, he admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair.

Initially , Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said there was nothing out of the ordinary about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang , an executive at a Singaporean datacenter firm, Megaspeed. US government officials had suspected Huang of smuggling American chips into China, prompting those officials to surveil and monitor her, the Times first reported. In the course of that surveillance, officials allegedly determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had gotten close with the Nvidia leader.

Nvidia’s board of directors have now launched an independent investigation about the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship.

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang wrote in his letter. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

Megaspeed did not respond to a Guardian request for comment before publication.

In his letter, Huang apologized to his family, acknowledging how much they’ve supported him. His wife, Mills, kept a relatively low profile and didn’t play a formal role at Nvidia. However, in a 2023 interview with the New Yorker, Huang shared that Mills had also worked in Silicon Valley as a microchips engineer before stepping away to raise their children.

“Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support,” Huang wrote in his letter to employees. “They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

Both his children now hold high ranking roles at the company, despite not initially pursuing careers in tech. His daughter, Madison, serves as the senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms, but got her start as a chef. She attended the Culinary Institute of America and Le Cordon Bleu before going to business school and transitioning to luxury marketing. She previously worked at LVMH – the parent company of Lous Vuitton.

Spencer , for his part, now serves as the director of product for Robotics at Nvidia but spent much of his career as a consultant before joining his father’s company as a product manager. Before consulting, he owned and co-founded a craft cocktail bar in Taiwan.

Could Jensen Huang be pushed out?

In his letter, Huang reiterated his commitment to Nvidia, saying he hoped to earn back his colleagues’ and employees’ trust. However, analysts and investors say there’s a chance he may be removed as CEO after the board’s investigation.

“This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” said Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at investment bank Yorkville Ives. “There is clearly risk as discussed that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.”

Ives said the family’s role at Nvidia adds some complexities for the board.

“The board has to make its decision independent of the family spider web of Jensen and his family at Nvidia,” Ives told the Guardian. “It makes this a very complex situation for the board to navigate with the world watching.”

after newsletter promotion

Huang is to Nvidia what Steve Jobs was to Apple, said Ken Mahoney, the CEO and president of Mahoney Asset Management. “If you asked any Nvidia investor or anyone involved in tech and markets, would they like to see Jensen gone? Definitely not, but [Nvidia] would survive,” Mahoney said.

“Losing Huang would introduce a lot of uncertainty, particularly given his influence over Nvidia’s strategy, culture, and relationships with major technology companies,” he continued. “The bigger question is whether a successor could maintain Huang’s strategic vision and ability to anticipate where the industry is heading, and how that new leader could be tested along the way if things become difficult.”

Executive affairs or inappropriate relationships have recently unseated CEOs, according to executive recruiting and coaching firm Challenger Gray and Christmas. In 2024, the CEO of Astronomer was caught on a kiss cam with the company’s chief people officer, leading him to resign shortly after. Nestlé fired CEO Laurent Freixe for a relationship with a subordinate.

Nvidia offers a more complex picture. On one hand, Huang’s affair is not just a matter morals or ethics, there are potential national security concerns. On the other, Huang is core to the DNA of Nvidia which in turn is the bedrock of the entire AI industry – an industry upon which the economy relies greatly.

Nvidia shares fell 7.5% as soon as the stock market opened, wiping over $330bn off the company’s value.

“When the CEO of the most valuable company in the world is tied to a counterintelligence investigation because of a personal relationship, every board in America should be paying attention,” said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas. “It’s not just a question of romance or morality any more. It’s a question of judgment, national security exposure, shareholder trust, and whether the person at the top can be relied on to protect the enterprise.”

In a statement, Nvidia’s board said they do not believe either national security or company secrets were compromised but they will “examine all available information.”

“The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” the board said in a statement .

stories.title: Sales of tinned food and bottled water jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
stories.summary: Sales of essential goods such as hand sanitiser soar after the government called on households to be prepared for emergencies.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 10 November 2026

Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.

Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.

The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.

Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.

Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.

Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.

Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".

The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".

Disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope previously told the BBC that the UK was playing "massive catch up" to other European nations in terms of preparedness.

These include France, Germany Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.

A number of experts have been calling for the UK to put more emphasis on food security, with some arguing that the government itself should take responsibility for food stockpiling, rather than individual households.

In October, a group of more than 180 experts signed an open letter , external to Burnham and first secretary of state Louise Haigh calling for local authorities to have a duty to prevent and respond to food supply emergencies.

They pointed out that a government survey found that 29% of people in the UK could not afford to keep a few days worth of food in the house.

stories.title: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
stories.summary: Huang, who is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, is far more important to the future of the world order than other tech bosses.

Watch: Jensen Huang speaks to the BBC's Faisal Islam in 2025

Published 10 November 2026

Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.

Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.

Both are innovators revered in the tech world. However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .

Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.

In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.

Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.

I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.

It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.

An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.

"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."

He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.

Differing views on security risks

However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.

Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.

The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.

He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.

Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".

He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".

What does this show us?

At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.

More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.

Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.

Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.

It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

stories.body:
Jensen Huang’s close relationship with president means Nvidia CEO’s affair with woman alleged to be working for Beijing is under intense scrutiny

A hand on the back, a kiss on the cheek; the footage of Alice Huang’s interaction with Jensen Huang in a Taipei venue last year does not seem particularly remarkable at first glance.

But the Nvidia chief executive’s revelation on Sunday that he had an affair with Ms Huang has given it new significance.

According to reports, his lover, who is not a relation, was not just an executive at an Nvidia customer. She was also an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia has now launched an independent investigation into reports that the boss of a cornerstone company in the global AI boom has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

“While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” said the board.

Huang, 63, a poster boy of the AI boom in his trademark leather jacket, admitted there was “no excuse” for what he had done.

Aside from Huang’s dented personal reputation, what is the scale of the damage done to Nvidia and US national security?

The story started to emerge last year when the New York Times and Bloomberg raised questions about a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia’s powerful chips, which have become the proverbial shovels in the AI gold rush. There were concerns that Megaspeed was flouting US restrictions on AI chip exports to China by diverting some Nvidia inventory to America’s arch AI rival. Nvidia and Megaspeed denied this.

Then last month came a further startling NYT report that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, and that American officials believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Donald Trump had been told, but decided not to act on the information. It is now evident that the relationship was more than just close.

At the heart of the question of what China might have achieved through Alice Huang is the extremely close relationship between the CEO of the world’s second-most-valuable company and the president of the United States.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia appeared to have successfully leaned on the US commerce department to halt an investigation into potential chip smuggling on the part of Megaspeed. That pressure came through a Trump appointee, who allowed Nvidia to reach out about the case.

Responding to reports last year that it might have diverted Nvidia deliveries, Megaspeed said: “Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company, operating fully in compliance with all applicable laws, including US export control regulations.”

Trump has met frequently – at least seven times – the head of Nvidia since the start of his second term. Huang has flown on Air Force One and taken calls from the president during public events.

Four of their meetings have touched on one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relationships: the controls that the US has put up around the export of the world’s most advanced AI chips, which are almost entirely sold by Nvidia.

Under the former president Joe Biden, the US put in place the Chips Act, a package of rules that introduced sweeping limitations on US tech companies and their overseas trading partners. These rules sought to control what semiconductor technologies US companies could sell to businesses based overseas – particularly those that might be put under pressure to transfer those technologies to China.

It also introduced strict licensing requirements that in turn limited what those partners could do with technology that they bought.

For Nvidia, this was bad for business. China was one of the largest markets for its GPU chips – accounting for roughly a quarter of its revenue in the years between 2020 and 2022. When the Chips Act passed, the company started to sell downgraded versions of its premier chips to China – for example , the A800 and H800. Some of these were then banned, forcing Nvidia to scramble even more.

Under Trump, things changed. The president first invited Huang to the White House just six days after he was inaugurated, to discuss AI policy and chip exports . The two then met again in July and August of 2025. This was followed by victories for Huang – Trump allowed Nvidia to export previously banned chips to China. Nvidia agreed, in turn, to give the US government 15% of the sales revenue.

Experts said the deal would help Beijing compete “on the AI frontier”, in other words develop AI systems to rival those being produced by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI.

Five months later, the tech boss appeared to win another startling concession, days after another meeting with Trump. The president agreed to allow the tech boss to export H200s – a far more powerful chip – to China, in exchange for 25% of the revenue.

“President Xi responded positively!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

It is not unusual for large technology companies to lobby for their preferred policies in Washington; nor is it unusual for Trump to give access – and favourable deals – to men he likes.

But one more thing is now apparent – during this crucial year for his company, Huang was also intimately involved with a reported Chinese spy. The two were first photographed together in mid-2024. Five months after Trump took office is when the two were filmed at the Taipei restaurant. This would have been at the height of Huang’s lobbying push, shortly before Trump agreed to let Nvidia sell the H200s.

What could Alice Huang have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair? Plenty. Glimpses into US policy as it was being made, and to Trump’s own chaotic thinking on AI. And perhaps a world of tips beyond the confines of the White House.

Huang was a key figure for government after government as they formulated their AI policy. He met world leaders from South Korea to Saudi Arabia that year; he joined the then UK prime minister Keir Starmer on stage in London.

He would have known the details of the most important tech policy for many governments on Earth – their AI ambitions – because his company was often the only one that could make these ambitions happen. That is certainly true for Britain.

For all the intellectual feats of the systems powered by Nvidia technology, it is Huang’s human intelligence that is most valuable to America’s competitors.

"He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang

Published 9 November 2026

US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.

Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.

The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.

According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy Published 1 day ago

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.

The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.

The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.

Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.

Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.

The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.

'An honourable guy'

At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.

"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.

He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.

The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.
